# Brucellosis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Infectious diseases > Zoonoses and vector-borne diseases > Brucellosis*

[Original Article Link](/library/lf0vm2)

---

## Summary

Brucellosis is a <u>zoonotic infection</u> caused by the <u>gram-negative coccobacillus</u> <u>Brucella</u>. In countries where brucellosis is <u>endemic</u>, the most common <u>vectors</u> are cattle, sheep, goats, and pigs. Transmission occurs through ingestion of contaminated animal products, contact with infected animals, or inhalation of <u>Brucella</u>. In the US, where livestock are routinely vaccinated, elk and bison are <u>vectors</u>, and locally acquired brucellosis is rare. Brucellosis typically manifests with <u>flu-like symptoms</u>. Other possible symptoms include <u>hepatomegaly</u>, <u>splenomegaly</u>, <u>lymphadenopathy</u>, and, rarely, focal organ infection (e.g., <u>osteomyelitis</u>, <u>endocarditis</u>, <u>spondylitis</u>). Diagnosis is based on positive cultures and/or <u>serology</u>. Treatment involves a combination <u>antibiotic</u> regimen based on disease severity. Prevention strategies include avoiding consumption of contaminated food, especially undercooked meat and unpasteurized dairy products, and contact with the tissues and fluids of infected animals; <u>postexposure prophylaxis</u> (PEP) with <u>antibiotics</u> may be recommended for individuals who have been exposed to <u>Brucella</u>.

---

## Etiology

* <u>Pathogen</u>: <u>Brucella</u> spp. are facultative intracellular, gram-negative, aerobic, coccobacilli.    [[1]](/library/D_W1qL0)

* Brucella melitensis: mainly affects sheep, goats, and camels → Malta <u>fever</u>

* Brucella abortus: mainly affects cattle, but also bison, deer, and elk → Bang disease

* Rare causes of disease in humans

* <u>Brucella</u> suis: mainly affects (feral and domestic) pigs and reindeer, but also cattle and bison

* <u>Brucella</u> canis: affects dogs

* Transmission: <u>zoonotic</u> [[1]](/library/D_W1qL0)

* Contaminated food, esp. raw meat, unpasteurized dairy products

* Contact with infected animals

* Exposure to aerosolized particles [[2]](/library/0zWerL0)

* <u>Risk factors</u>: occupational or recreational exposure to infected animals and animal products (e.g., farmers, veterinarians, hunters, slaughterhouse workers, laboratory personnel)

* Pathophysiology: <u>Brucella</u> spp. survive and replicate within <u>macrophages</u> of the <u>reticuloendothelial system</u> → formation of <u>noncaseating granulomas</u>





![Brucella melitensis](media/apuzx3z9zz2yniahdjvkkaes.jpg)

## Clinical features

* <u>Incubation period</u>: commonly 2–4 weeks (ranges from 5 days to 6 months) [[1]](/library/D_W1qL0)

* General [[2]](/library/0zWerL0)

* <u>Flu-like symptoms</u>

* Night sweats

* High, potentially <u>undulant fever</u>

* Painful <u>lymphadenopathy</u>

* <u>Hepatomegaly</u>

* <u>Splenomegaly</u> [[2]](/library/0zWerL0)

* Localized infection

* <u>Arthralgias</u>, <u>low back pain</u> → osteoarticular infection (e.g., <u>osteomyelitis</u>, <u>spondylitis</u>)

* Epididymal and testicular tenderness, flank <u>pain</u> → genitourinary infection ; (e.g., <u>epididymo-orchitis</u>, <u>pyelonephritis</u>)

* <u>Murmurs</u>, friction rubs, <u>tachycardia</u> → cardiac infection (e.g., <u>endocarditis</u>, <u>myocarditis</u>)

* Additional symptoms may be present as <u>Brucella</u> can infect any organ.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Brucellosis in pregnancy</u> can cause <u>spontaneous abortion</u>, <u>preterm labor</u>, and <u>stillbirth</u>. [[3]](/library/Bedza60)




> [!NOTE]
> Brucellosis manifests as UNdulant <u>fever</u> and the causative <u>pathogen</u> is transmitted by UNpasteurized dairy products.

---

## Diagnosis

Suspect brucellosis in adults and children with relevant exposure history, especially if common causes of symptoms have been ruled out and symptoms persist (e.g., in culture-negative <u>endocarditis</u>, <u>CNS</u> involvement). [[1]](/library/D_W1qL0)[[3]](/library/Bedza60)




### General principles




* Obtain confirmatory studies (e.g., <u>blood cultures</u>, <u>serology</u>) in all patients with suspected brucellosis.

* Consider additional directed studies (e.g., tissue <u>biopsy</u>, <u>CSF</u> culture) in patients with localized infection.

* Isolation of <u>Brucella</u> from a culture or a rise in <u>antibody</u> <u>titers</u> over 2 weeks confirms the diagnosis.





> [!TIP]
> Diagnosing brucellosis can be challenging due to nonspecific symptoms and potential to impact any organ.




> [!WARNING]
> When submitting cultures, inform laboratory personnel of suspected <u>Brucella</u>, as additional protective equipment and precautions are required when handling <u>Brucella</u> specimens. [[1]](/library/D_W1qL0)




### Routine <u>laboratory studies</u> [[2]](/library/0zWerL0)[[4]](/library/azWQrL0)[[5]](/library/gOdF7J0)




Findings are nonspecific but may support the diagnosis.




* <u>CBC</u>

* <u>Anemia</u>

* <u>Leukopenia</u> or <u>leukocytosis</u>, <u>lymphocytosis</u>, <u>eosinopenia</u>

* <u>Thrombocytopenia</u> or <u>thrombocytosis</u>

* <u>Pancytopenia</u> (rare)

* <u>BMP</u>: elevated <u>creatinine</u> (uncommon) [[6]](/library/2zWTHL0)

* <u>Liver</u> enzymes: <u>mildly elevated transaminases</u>

* <u>CPK</u>: may be elevated  [[6]](/library/2zWTHL0)





### Confirmatory studies [[1]](/library/D_W1qL0)[[2]](/library/0zWerL0)[[3]](/library/Bedza60)




* <u>Serology</u>  [[1]](/library/D_W1qL0)[[7]](/library/9_WNqL0)

* Methods

* Agglutination tests, e.g., serum agglutination test, <u>Brucella</u> microagglutination test, <u>Rose Bengal test</u>

* <u>ELISA</u>

* Confirmatory findings: fourfold rise in <u>titers</u> from samples taken ≥ 2 weeks apart  [[2]](/library/0zWerL0)[[8]](/library/x_WEqL0)

* Direct detection

* <u>Blood culture</u> (<u>false negatives</u> often occur): should be incubated for ≥ 10–14 days  [[1]](/library/D_W1qL0)

* Tissue <u>biopsy</u> with <u>histopathology</u> and culture

* Specimen

* <u>Bone marrow</u> (<u>gold standard</u>)  [[2]](/library/0zWerL0)

* Other affected areas, e.g., <u>lymph node</u>, <u>CSF</u>

* <u>Histopathology</u>: <u>noncaseating granulomas</u> [[9]](/library/RzWlsL0)

* Culture medium for isolation, e.g., <u>charcoal yeast extract agar</u> (<u>cysteine</u> and <u>iron</u> buffered) [[10]](/library/oPX0fy)

* <u>NAAT</u> (e.g., <u>PCR</u>): detection of <u>Brucella</u> <u>DNA</u> in tissue or serum sample [[8]](/library/x_WEqL0)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Brucella</u> cultures require prolonged incubation. [[1]](/library/D_W1qL0)[[3]](/library/Bedza60)

---

## Treatment

### Approach




* Consult infectious diseases (ID) to help guide <u>antibiotic therapy</u>.

* Notify the local health department.

* Use appropriate <u>PPE</u> (see “<u>Prevention of brucellosis</u>”).

* Arrange <u>PEP for brucellosis</u> contacts as needed.

* Refer to <u>surgery</u> for deep tissue infections and complicated infections (e.g., <u>abscess</u>, <u>spinal instability</u>). [[1]](/library/D_W1qL0)[[11]](/library/eZdx0o0)

* For infections in children and pregnant individuals, see “Special patient groups.”





> [!WARNING]
> Brucellosis is a nationally <u>notifiable disease</u> in the US. Notify your local health department if a case is confirmed.




### <u>Antibiotic therapy</u> [[1]](/library/D_W1qL0)[[12]](/library/UZdbao0)




#### Uncomplicated infection




* <u>Doxycycline</u> DOSAGE for 6 weeks  [[8]](/library/x_WEqL0)[[12]](/library/UZdbao0)

* PLUS one of the following: ;  [[1]](/library/D_W1qL0)[[12]](/library/UZdbao0)

* <u>Aminoglycoside</u>  [[2]](/library/0zWerL0)[[11]](/library/eZdx0o0); 

* <u>Streptomycin</u> DOSAGE for 2–3 weeks

* OR <u>gentamicin</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE for 1–2 weeks [[12]](/library/UZdbao0)

* OR <u>rifampin</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE for 6 weeks [[8]](/library/x_WEqL0)[[12]](/library/UZdbao0)





#### Complicated infection  [[8]](/library/x_WEqL0)[[11]](/library/eZdx0o0)[[12]](/library/UZdbao0)




Complicated brucellosis infection refers to deep-seated or focal infection, e.g.:




* Neurobrucellosis  [[13]](/library/hZdcYo0)

* <u>Ceftriaxone</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[11]](/library/eZdx0o0)

* PLUS <u>doxycycline</u> DOSAGE

* PLUS <u>rifampin</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[8]](/library/x_WEqL0)

* <u>Endocarditis</u>

* <u>Aminoglycoside</u>: <u>streptomycin</u> DOSAGE OR <u>gentamicin</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[12]](/library/UZdbao0)

* PLUS <u>doxycycline</u> DOSAGE

* PLUS <u>rifampin</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[8]](/library/x_WEqL0)

* <u>Spondylitis</u>

* <u>Doxycycline</u> DOSAGE

* PLUS an <u>aminoglycoside</u>: e.g., <u>streptomycin</u> DOSAGE





> [!TIP]
> Complicated infections often require three-drug therapy and/or a long treatment duration (e.g., 4–6 months). [[11]](/library/eZdx0o0)
